736.title: The garden, fully told (Confessions 8)
736.hook: weeping under a fig tree, he hears take and read and opens Romans 13
736.howItsDone: Catholics read scripture at Mass, where the readings follow a set cycle, and on their own; lectio divina, a slow, prayerful reading of a short passage, is one way the Church encourages people to read it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Milan, where Augustine went to judge Ambrose's speaking and the substance got in. Your line was came for the style.

The garden of the house where Augustine is staying in Milan. Two friends have gone out there to get away from people: Augustine and his friend Alypius. Augustine is in pieces. He has heard the sermons. He has run out of arguments. What's left, he says, is his own will, split in two, wanting God and wanting his old life, both at once. He gets up, leaves Alypius sitting with a book of Paul's letters, goes off alone, and throws himself down under a fig tree. And he cries.
screen: `A GARDEN IN MILAN.` → `A WILL SPLIT IN TWO.` → `UNDER A FIG TREE, WEEPING.`

segments.voice: Augustine gives us his own words from under that tree, in the Latin of the Confessions: quamdiu, quamdiu, cras et cras? How long, how long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now? Why not an end to it this very hour? Then he hears a voice from a house nearby, like a boy's or a girl's, chanting over and over: tolle lege, tolle lege. Take and read, take and read. He stops crying long enough to think. Is this some children's game? He can't remember any game with those words. So he takes it as a command: open the book, and read the first passage you find. He remembers what he'd been told: how Anthony of the desert walked into church, heard a Gospel being read, and took it as spoken straight to him. So Augustine goes back to where Alypius is sitting, picks up the book of Paul's letters, opens it, and reads in silence the first passage his eyes fall on. It's Romans thirteen. Not in rioting and drunkenness, it says, not in impurity, not in quarreling. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He read no further, and didn't need to. It was as if light flooded his heart and the darkness of doubt ran off. He marks the place with his finger and tells Alypius. Alypius asks to see, reads the next line, about receiving the one who is weak in faith, and takes it for himself. Then the two of them go straight inside to tell Monica. Augustine says she was overjoyed. Her tears had been answered.

737.title: At the window in Ostia (Confessions 9)
737.hook: mother and son talk of heaven at a window, and days later she dies
737.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Monica and Saint Augustine on neighboring feast days, and Monica's request to be remembered at the altar is often recalled when Mass is offered for those who have died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the garden in Milan: a child's voice chanting take and read, and Augustine opening Paul's letter. Your line was take and read.

A port town at the mouth of the Tiber. A house with a small garden, and two people leaning on a windowsill, looking down into it, tired from a long road and waiting for a ship home to Africa. One is Augustine, newly baptized. The other is his mother, Monica, who prayed and wept for him for years. Nobody else is in the room. Nothing is planned. They just start talking. And by Augustine's own account, somewhere in that unplanned conversation, the two of them, for a moment, touch the very thing they're talking about.
screen: `A HOUSE AT OSTIA.` → `MOTHER AND SON AT THE WINDOW.` → `A CONVERSATION NOBODY PLANNED.`

segments.voice: First, the subject. In book nine of the Confessions, Augustine says they asked each other what the eternal life of the saints would be like, the life Paul says no eye has seen and no ear has heard. Not small talk. Second, the climb. As they talk, their minds rise past everything made: past the earth, the sky and the stars, past their own minds, until for one heartbeat they touch the wisdom by which all things were made. Then they sigh, and come back down to the noise of human words, which begin and end. He doesn't claim they stayed there. It was a moment, and they wanted it to last. Third, what Monica says afterward. Son, nothing in this life delights me anymore. There was one thing I wanted to stay alive for: to see you a Catholic Christian before I died. God has given me that and more. What am I still doing here? Fourth, the ending. A few days later she falls ill with a fever. She tells her sons not to worry about where her body is buried. Lay it anywhere, she says. Only remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you are. And she dies there, far from home. Augustine held back his tears at the funeral, and wept later, alone, before God. So the window isn't only a mystical peak. It's two people who loved each other, saying what mattered while there was still time.

738.title: Late have I loved thee (Confessions 10.27)
738.hook: too late loved I thee, O thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new
738.howItsDone: Catholics hear this passage from the Confessions in the Office of Readings on the feast of Saint Augustine, and some pray its lines on their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the window at Ostia: Monica and Augustine talking about heaven, days before she died. Your line was the window at ostia.

Late. It's a word with a sting in it. Late for the train. Late with the apology. Too late to say it to someone who's gone. In book ten of the Confessions, Augustine has finished telling the story of his past and turns to who he is now. Partway through, the word he reaches for is that one. Late. Read on a few lines, though, and it isn't a cry of despair. It turns into something closer to a love letter.
screen: `LATE.` → `BOOK TEN: WHO HE IS NOW.` → `ONE PARAGRAPH, SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: First, the opening, in Edward Pusey's old English translation: "Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee!" In Augustine's Latin: sero te amavi, pulchritudo tam antiqua et tam nova. Beauty so ancient and so new. God isn't called judge here, or king. God is called beauty, older than anything and fresh as this morning. Second, where he'd been looking. You were within, he says, and I was outside, and there I searched for you. He'd hunted through the lovely things God had made, as if they were the end of the road. Then one short line: "Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee." The distance was never on God's side. Third, how God broke through, sense by sense. You called and shouted, and broke through my deafness. You flashed and shone, and scattered my blindness. You breathed fragrance, and I drew in my breath and now I long for you. I tasted, and now I hunger and thirst. You touched me, and I burned for your peace. The same senses that had kept him busy outside become the way God reaches him. Fourth, why late isn't the last word. He says late twice; he doesn't pretend the lost years away. But everything after it is about being found. Late, here, isn't too late. It's the honest start of a love already under way.

739.title: The City of God (after 410)
739.hook: Rome is sacked, and Augustine writes of two cities built by two loves
739.tomorrow: Love, and do what you will
739.howItsDone: When the Second Vatican Council describes the Church in Lumen Gentium 8, it quotes The City of God on the Church pressing forward like a pilgrim, amid the world's persecutions and God's consolations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, late have I loved thee, and God called pulchritudo, beauty. Your line was ever ancient, ever new.

News crosses the sea to North Africa: Rome has been sacked by the Goths. Not a border town. Rome. The city that had seemed as permanent as the sky. Refugees arrive with stories. And some who still honor the old gods say out loud what others are whispering: this is what happens when an empire abandons its gods for the Christian one. Augustine, a bishop in a harbor town, hears it. He doesn't answer with a quick sermon. He starts writing, book after book, until the answer becomes the work he calls The City of God.
screen: `ROME HAS BEEN SACKED.` → `THEY BLAME THE CHRISTIANS.` → `AUGUSTINE STARTS TO WRITE.`

segments.voice: First, the question underneath. If God is on our side, how could Rome fall? Augustine moves the ground. No city on earth was ever God's guarantee. Empires rise and fall; something else is being built. Second, the heart of it, in book fourteen. Two loves, he says, have made two cities. The earthly city is built by love of self, reaching even to contempt of God. The heavenly city is built by love of God, reaching even to contempt of self. The line runs by love, not by address. Rome is not simply the earthly city. And though Augustine can call the Church the city of God, he says that on earth even the Church holds some who will not share its end, while some of its present enemies will. Third, in this world the two cities are mixed together, tangled, until the last judgment. Some readers hear Jesus's parable of the wheat and the weeds in that. You can't draw a map. The same street, the same family, sometimes the same heart, holds both loves pulling against each other. Fourth, how to live in the meantime. Augustine calls the city of God a pilgrim on earth. Pilgrims don't despise the towns they pass through. They use the roads, keep the peace, pray for the place, the way the prophet Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon to seek the peace of the city. But they don't mistake it for home. For Augustine, Rome's fall was terrible and real, but not the end of the story. For him, the city that mattered most had never had walls.

segments.voice: Look back over the last day at three things you did with real effort: a task, a conversation, a decision. For each, ask gently: which love was doing the building, love of self, or love turned toward God or someone else's good? A day can hold both; if you pray, offer tomorrow's work to God.

740.title: Love, and do what you will
740.hook: Augustine's sermon line: if love is the root, only good can grow
740.howItsDone: Catholic preachers and teachers who quote Augustine's line from his homilies on First John tend to set it back in its sermon, where he spells it out as a test of motives: keep quiet, cry out, correct or spare, but from love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, The City of God, civitas Dei: two loves, two cities, tangled together until the end. Your line was two loves, two cities.

It shows up on posters, in wedding speeches, sometimes tattooed on a forearm. Love, and do what you will. On its own, it can sound like permission for anything: feel it, then follow it. But the line wasn't written for a poster. Augustine said it in a sermon on the First Letter of John, to a church in North Africa. In context it's close to the opposite of anything goes. Augustine makes it a test, and a harder one than any rulebook.
screen: `A POSTER LINE.` → `A SERMON ON FIRST JOHN.` → `HARDER THAN A RULEBOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the letter he's preaching on. First John says it plainly. In the Douay-Rheims: "He that loveth not, knoweth not God: for God is charity." If God is love, Augustine reasons, then love isn't one virtue among many. It's the root. Second, his example. A father corrects his son sternly. A kidnapper speaks to the boy sweetly. Judge by the outside, and the kidnapper looks kinder. Judge by the root, and the father is the one who loves. The same action, he says, can come from love or from its opposite. Third, the line itself, in Latin: dilige, et quod vis fac. Love, and do what you will. Then he spells it out. If you keep quiet, keep quiet from love. If you cry out, cry out from love. If you correct someone, correct from love. If you spare someone, spare from love. Let the root of love be within, he says, and from that root nothing but good can grow. Fourth, why this is harder. A rule asks: did you do the right thing? Augustine asks: why did you do it? You can follow every rule and still act from pride, or spite, or fear. And you can't fake a root. So love, and do what you will isn't a loophole. It's an inspection, down below the soil, where only you and God can see.
screen: `GOD IS CHARITY.` · `THE FATHER AND THE KIDNAPPER.` · `DILIGE, ET QUOD VIS FAC.` · `NOT A LOOPHOLE. AN INSPECTION.` · then, large: `LOVE, THEN DO.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you'll do anyway today, a reply to a message, making dinner, telling someone no, and ask Augustine's question: what's the root? If it's irritation, or wanting to look good, look for a second root underneath, real care for the person or the task, and rest there for a few breaths. If you pray, ask God for that love before you begin.

741.title: Jerome in Bethlehem (c. 347–420)
741.hook: a prickly scholar translates the Bible into everyday Latin
741.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Jerome as a Doctor of the Church and a patron of translators and scripture scholars, and the Douay-Rheims English Bible was translated from the Latin Vulgate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's sermon line: love, and do what you will. Your carry was love, then do.

A young scholar falls sick with a fever, and dreams he's dragged before the judgment seat. A voice asks who he is. A Christian, he answers. You lie, says the voice. Ciceronianus es, non Christianus. You're a Ciceronian, not a Christian. The scholar is Jerome, and he tells this dream himself in a letter. He loved Cicero's polished Latin and found the plain style of the Bible hard to stomach. Strange, then, that this is the man who spent his later years in Bethlehem putting the Bible into plain Latin for ordinary churchgoers.
screen: `A FEVER AND A DREAM.` → `A CICERONIAN, NOT A CHRISTIAN.` → `THEN, A BIBLE FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Jerome's letters show a brilliant, restless, sharp-tongued scholar, warm with friends and fierce with opponents. Holiness, in his case, didn't come with a soft personality. Second, the problem he was asked to fix. Latin-speaking Christians had Bibles, but the old Latin versions differed from copy to copy. A pope asked Jerome to revise the Gospels, and the work grew from there. Third, the bold step. For the Old Testament, Jerome went back behind the Greek to the Hebrew. In Bethlehem he worked at it, and he says he learned Hebrew from a Jewish teacher who came to him by night. Not everyone was pleased. Augustine wrote to him, worried that a new wording in the book of Jonah had upset a congregation that knew the old one by heart. Familiar words are hard to give up. Fourth, what it became. His translation, along with other parts of the old Latin, came to be called the Vulgate. And here's the thread that reaches you: the Douay-Rheims, the English Bible quoted on this path, was translated from Jerome's Latin. So when you hear "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," you're hearing Jerome, one step removed. In his Latin: In principio erat Verbum. The common tongue, for the common church.
screen: `A SHARP-TONGUED SAINT.` · `THE OLD LATIN COPIES DIFFERED.` · `BACK TO THE HEBREW, IN BETHLEHEM.` · `THE BIBLE IN COMMON LATIN.` · then, large: `IN PRINCIPIO ERAT VERBUM.`

segments.voice: Say the first line of John's Gospel in Jerome's Latin, slowly, even if you've never studied Latin: In principio erat Verbum. In the beginning was the Word. Say the Latin once more and notice which words you can already guess, principio, beginning, verbum, word, or say the verse in another language you speak at home, and let the strange sound slow you down; if you pray, rest on that one line.
Vulgate. Jerome's Latin Bible, revised from the Greek and, in Bethlehem, translated from the Hebrew, for ordinary Latin-speaking churches. Today's word.

742.title: Ignorance of scripture
742.hook: Jerome: not knowing the scriptures is not knowing Christ (CCC 133)
742.howItsDone: The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes Jerome's line when it urges the faithful to read scripture often, and some Catholics keep a daily habit of reading the day's Mass readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vulgate: Jerome in Bethlehem, putting the Bible into the common tongue. Your line was the common tongue.

Count the open books this week. Augustine in a garden, hearing take and read, and opening Paul. Augustine and Monica at a window, talking about a life no eye has seen, words Paul quotes. Late have I loved thee, his story turned into prayer. The City of God, sending pilgrims to Jeremiah's advice. Love, then do, preached on First John. And Jerome, giving the book a common tongue. Again and again, the page is close at hand. Jerome says why, in one sentence the Catechism still quotes.
screen: `A WEEK OF OPEN BOOKS.` → `AGAIN AND AGAIN, THE PAGE.` → `JEROME SAYS WHY.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. Jerome wrote it at the start of his commentary on the prophet Isaiah. In his Latin: ignoratio Scripturarum ignoratio Christi est. Ignorance of the scriptures is ignorance of Christ. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it in its section on scripture, and so did the Second Vatican Council. Second, how he gets there. It isn't a slogan; it's an argument in two steps. Jesus told his hearers to search the scriptures, because they bear witness to him. And Paul calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. So, Jerome reasons, if you don't know the scriptures, you don't know God's power and God's wisdom, and that means you don't know Christ. Third, why put this line at the front of a book on Isaiah, an ancient prophet? Jerome says Isaiah speaks so clearly of Christ that he reads less like a prophet than a gospel writer. Fourth, what this asks of an ordinary reader. Not a degree. Jerome wrote this commentary at the request of a woman who studied scripture with him, not for a faculty. Some readers put it this way: knowing scripture is like knowing a friend. You learn the voice by listening often. You can know a lot about someone and still not know them. Read like that, the line is less a scolding than an invitation: for Jerome, time with the book is time with Christ.
screen: `IGNORATIO SCRIPTURARUM.` · `SEARCH THE SCRIPTURES; CHRIST IS WISDOM.` · `ISAIAH, ALMOST A GOSPEL.` · `LEARN THE VOICE BY LISTENING.` · then, large: `KNOW THE BOOK, KNOW HIM.`

segments.voice: Open a Bible, or a Bible app, to any of the four Gospels; Mark is short, if you want somewhere to start. Read one page slowly, without trying to study it, just listening for the voice: what Jesus says, what he does, who he's talking to. Then go back to one line that caught you and stay with it, and if you pray, ask to know him through what you've read.
Jerome. The scholar who wrote that ignorance of the scriptures is ignorance of Christ, in his prologue to the prophet Isaiah. Today's word.
Your line: know the book, know him. One page at a time is enough. See you tomorrow.
